strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies path regularity as the primary computational bottleneck in Neural CDEs with rigorous theoretical grounding (Theorem 3.1)
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorems 3.1-3.4 establish relationships between path smoothness and NFE, with Corollary 3.3 quantifying h^{-1} scaling
Substantial practical improvements: Achieves 4.3×-14.5× speedups in inference while maintaining SOTA or competitive accuracy across three datasets
Creative architecture design: Multi-view framework with learned queries to recover smoothing-induced information loss is well-motivated, inspired by Q-Former but applied innovatively

Comprehensive experimental methodology: Includes ablation studies, noise robustness analysis, attention visualization, computational cost breakdown, and fair baseline comparisons with consistent hyperparameters
Thorough presentation: Well-organized with extensive appendices covering theoretical proofs and experimental reproducibility details
weaknesses: Informal core theoretical statements: Theorem 3.1 marked 'informal' despite being central; the claimed scaling ‖d^{p+1}z/dt^{p+1}‖ ∝ ‖d^{p+1}X/dt^{p+1}‖ depends on f_θ's Lipschitz constant only parenthetically mentioned, requiring formalization
Limited experimental scope: Only 3 datasets from UEA/UCR archives; claims of 'state-of-the-art' lack breadth; no evaluation on longer sequences (>500 steps) or other problem types (e.g., forecasting)

Unclear advantage over simpler baselines: GRU-D achieves 96.57% vs MVC-GP's 98.28% on SpokenArabicDigits; paper doesn't clarify when Neural CDEs justify their complexity; comparable wall-clock times on some tasks

Information recovery lacking formal justification: No theoretical analysis proving multiple smoothed trajectories with attention preserve task-relevant information; diminishing returns at M=4 suggest practical limits without theoretical motivation

Weighted GP formulation under-justified (Eq. 4): Setting noise variance inversely proportional to attention scores lacks principled justification; why is this weighting optimal? Sensitivity analysis missing

Theorem 3.4 bottleneck tension: Shows NFE ∝ (min_m h_m)^{-1}, yet paper claims balancing 'representation capability with integration speed'—this fundamental tension unresolved; fine scales add cost, creating design contradictions

Design choices lack justification: Bandwidth sweep [0.01, 9.0] appears ad-hoc; CNN architecture (2-layer, kernel 3) arbitrary; M=4 based on empirical diminishing returns with no principled criterion; solver tolerance varies across datasets without explanation
Inconsistent hyperparameters in Table 1: MVC-GP CharacterTrajectories uses BW:[166.6, 166.6, 166.6, 166.6]—identical across heads, contradicting heterogeneous initialization advocacy
Missing scalability analysis: O(N³) GP matrix inversion not addressed; memory overhead of M trajectories not discussed; no evaluation on sequences >1000 steps

Incomplete baseline analysis: Log-NCDE comparison could be deeper; GRU-D sometimes outperforms, raising questions about Neural CDE necessity; no comparison to other smoothing methods (LOESS, spline smoothing)

strengths: Clear problem motivation with well-illustrated solver stiffness issue in Neural CDEs
Comprehensive experimental appendices with detailed hyperparameters and ablation studies
Convincing noise robustness analysis (Figure 4) demonstrating advantages of smoothing-based approaches
Extensive ablations on head count and smoothing parameters with informative visualizations
Thorough treatment of attention weight visualization providing interpretability insights
weaknesses: Critical inconsistency: Theorem 3.4 claims min_m h_m dominates NFE, but empirical results show multi-head models substantially outperform single-head models despite this bottleneck—no adequate theoretical explanation provided
Unfair baseline comparisons: non-CDE baselines use different hyperparameters than proposed methods, and accuracy levels differ significantly, making direct comparison invalid
Limited theoretical novelty: Theorems 3.1-3.3 are standard results from numerical analysis and kernel methods; primary contribution reduces to smoothing + attention, which is incremental
Experimental scope too limited: only 3 small UEA datasets (N<9000), no statistical significance testing, missing comparisons to recent Neural CDE variants and modern sequence models

Wall-clock time claims misleading: preprocessing shifts work to initialization phase; on SpokenArabicDigits, MVC-GP (7.32s) is 3.6× slower than GRU-D (2.02s); speedup comes primarily from shifting computation
Design choices lack justification: heteroscedastic GP noise variance as inverse attention weights is ad-hoc; unclear why attention on raw features is necessary versus learnable parameters alone
Missing fair accuracy-matched comparisons: Cubic (86.61%) vs MVC-GP (95.07%) are fundamentally different models; should compare models at similar accuracy levels

strengths: Clear problem identification: diagnoses that adaptive solvers are forced to track high-frequency variations in noisy interpolations, supported by rigorous Theorem 3.1 connecting control path regularity to NFE

Rigorous theoretical analysis with well-derived theorems (3.1-3.4) and mathematical proofs in appendices showing GPsensure optimal linear reconstruction and characterizing the parallel integration bottleneck

Elegant technical solution combining kernel/GP smoothing with attention-based multi-view reconstruction; heteroscedastic GP formulation (Eq. 4) using attention scores to modulate noise variance is particularly creative

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: fair comparison with consistent hyperparameters, thorough ablations on head count/bandwidth, and compelling noise robustness analysis showing smoothing methods maintain constant NFE under perturbation while interpolation methods degrade

Substantial practical improvements demonstrated: 4.3-14.5× speedups over standard Neural CDEs while achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, directly addressing a known computational bottleneck in the field
Well-written paper with clear presentation, good motivation, informative figures (especially Figure 2 and 4), and useful 'temporal parallelization' interpretation that provides good intuition
Proper experimental methodology: train/val/test splits, channel-wise normalization on training data only, multiple random seeds (5), consistent solver configuration across methods
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: only 3 datasets, all relatively small (max 8,800 sequences); evaluation restricted to classification tasks with no forecasting, regression, or extrapolation experiments

Fundamental bottleneck revealed by Theorem 3.4 (NFE_total ∝ min_m h_m^{-1}) severely constrains multi-view design—adding heads with diverse smoothing parameters doesn't help if any is stiff; the practical implications and design guidance for practitioners needs clarification

Incomplete design justification: CNN architecture in MVC-CDE (2-layer, kernel 3, 128 units), query initialization, and dimension d_ctx appear arbitrary with no ablations; hyperparameter sensitivity analysis missing

Unexplained performance anomalies: Log-NCDE dramatically underperforms on UWaveGestureLibrary (70.91% vs 95.39%); GRU-D achieves 96.57% on SpokenArabicDigits in 2.02s vs MVC-GP 98.28% in 7.32s—raises questions about method selection guidance

Computational cost opacity: Figure 10 shows training time improvements but total wall-clock time includes GP O(N³) preprocessing—the claim that this is 'negligible' (page 4) needs careful justification, especially for single-shot inference applications

Limited novelty in core techniques: kernel smoothing and GP regression are classical; contribution is primarily their application to Neural CDEs combined with standard multi-head attention, positioning this as more of an engineering contribution than fundamental advance

Reproducibility gaps: no code availability mentioned; bandwidth sweep range [0.01, 9.0] and h_eff = h_raw × T_max scaling lack justification; rectilinear padding strategy may bias variable-length sequence results

Missing key ablations and comparisons: no systematic isolation of smoothing alone vs smoothing+single attention vs multi-head effects; no experimental comparison to other cited regularization techniques (Kelly et al. 2020, Finlay et al. 2020) despite mentioning them

strengths: Sound theoretical foundation with rigorous connection between control path regularity and NFE via L^{1/(p+1)}-norm analysis (Theorems 3.1-3.4)
Clear problem identification: spline interpolation creates solver stiffness; excellent visualization of the issue and its severity under noise (Figure 1, Figure 4)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations on head count, bandwidth, solver order, and robustness to irregular sampling; noise robustness analysis (Figure 4) particularly convincing
Practical speedups demonstrated: 5-14× over standard Neural CDEs with competitive accuracy on multiple benchmarks
Dual-path approach well-designed: single-path smoothing baselines provide clear ablation; multi-view architecture addresses information loss with attention mechanism
Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, parameter matching between models, multiple random seeds, memory reporting (Table 3)
Interpretability analysis: attention weight visualization (Figure 5) shows dataset-specific patterns; computational cost breakdown (Figure 10) transparent
Heteroscedastic GP formulation (Eq. 4) elegantly incorporates attention weights into noise modeling
weaknesses: Bandwidth selection introduces significant hyperparameter tuning burden, undermining 'decoupling' claims: Table 2 shows extreme ranges (h ∈ [1.95, 166.6]), contradicting claims of task-aware parameterization without per-dataset validation

Weak comparison with state-of-the-art: Mamba achieves 96.64% accuracy on CharacterTrajectories with 31.16s training vs. MVC-GP's 95.07% with 22.63s; wall-clock speedup claims don't account for setup overhead; Pareto frontiers (Figure 3) show considerable overlap

Memory overhead significant but downplayed: MVC-GP uses 2-2.5× more memory than baseline CDEs (375 MB vs 152 MB) despite claims of efficiency; only compared favorably to Mamba, not other continuous-time models

Causal processing limitation inadequately addressed: GP/kernel smoothing require full-sequence access; proposed rolling-window solution introduces batch-level latency contradicting continuous-time processing claims (Section 4.2)
Theorem 3.4 bottleneck unresolved: NFE scales with min_m h_m; one stiff head bottlenecks entire system; no algorithmic solution proposed (e.g., heterogeneous per-head tolerances not explored)
Limited scope: method specific to Neural CDEs; applicability to other ODE-based architectures or fixed-step solvers unclear; restricted evaluation of when approach fails

Information loss not fully characterized: acknowledged loss of high-frequency features (Section 5), but only one generative task (ETTm1) evaluated; unclear applicability to fault detection, signal processing, or other frequency-critical applications

Dataset diversity limited: only 3 main benchmarks, all relatively small (≤8,800 sequences); PEMS-SF is high-dimensional but only 440 samples; no evaluation on modern large-scale time-series benchmarks

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying path roughness as a computational bottleneck in Neural CDEs, with theoretical characterization via Theorem 3.1
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets with detailed ablations, noise robustness analysis, and computational cost breakdowns
Practical efficiency gains of 5-14× speedup over standard CDEs while maintaining competitive accuracy
Extensive reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and component-wise analysis in appendices
Robustness validation under noise, irregular sampling, different ODE solver orders, and high-dimensional settings
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applies standard smoothing techniques (kernels, GPs) from classical statistics to CDEs with simple Q-Former-style attention; core insight is straightforward once problem is identified

Weak theoretical contributions: Theorems 3.1-3.3 are direct restatements of existing ODE solver theory (Hairer et al. 1993) and approximation theory (Wand & Jones 1995); Theorem 3.4 is relatively straightforward; overall contributions are pedagogical rather than novel

Unresolved trade-offs: (1) Bandwidth h requires validation tuning, shifting rather than solving the hyperparameter problem; (2) Frequency information loss is acknowledged but not resolved, with multi-view approach adding complexity to compensate; (3) Offline preprocessing requirement is presented as afterthought despite being significant for streaming scenarios; (4) Memory overhead 2.5× higher than baselines deserves more discussion

Fairness concerns in experimental comparisons: different baselines require different hyperparameter tuning (Section B.4), capacity-matching is inconsistent across models, and results show concerning disparities (e.g., GRU-D very strong on some datasets while weak on others)

Limited baselines: primarily compares against older CDE variants and legacy RNNs (GRU-D 2016, ODE-RNN 2019); missing comparisons with recent Transformers, other CDE efficiency methods, and recent smoothing-based ODE approaches; Mamba is included but represents different problem domain

Unclear multi-view mechanism benefit: ablation shows modest gains (1-8% depending on dataset), diversity regularization experiments (Section C.4) show forced diversity actually hurts performance (87.5% vs 92%), suggesting heads don't learn complementary roles

Incomplete applicability analysis: no clear characterization of which time series types benefit most/least from smoothing; when would exact interpolation be preferable; heterogeneous results across datasets not adequately explained

Presentation and scope: paper is dense with key details relegated to appendices; datasets are relatively small standard benchmarks; time series classification is somewhat dated compared to more relevant long-horizon forecasting tasks

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation with Theorems 3.1-3.4 rigorously establishing the relationship between control path regularity and solver efficiency, providing principled justification for the proposed smoothing approach

Novel multi-view architecture design that elegantly addresses information loss from over-smoothing via learnable attention queries, with heterogeneous bandwidth initialization enabling multi-scale representation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with fair capacity-matched baselines, thorough ablations (head count, bandwidth strategies, noise robustness, solver orders, irregular sampling), and evaluation on diverse datasets including high-dimensional PEMS-SF
Significant practical improvements: 5-14× NFE reduction and comparable/superior accuracy compared to standard Neural CDEs, with strong robustness to noise and missing data
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, effective visualizations, interpretable attention weight analysis, and honest limitations discussion; reproducibility details provided in appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: kernel smoothing and GP smoothing are standard techniques; Q-Former inspired attention mechanism borrowed from prior work; main contribution is their combination, which while well-executed is somewhat incremental

Bandwidth hyperparameter tuning not fully resolved: introduces new hyperparameter requiring validation set tuning via log-spaced search (0.01-9.0), adding computational overhead that partially undermines efficiency claims

Offline path construction limitation: requires access to full sequence for GP/kernel smoothing; while rolling windows discussed for forecasting (Appendix B.7), this deviates from true online processing and limits applicability to streaming scenarios

Insufficient theoretical justification for attention mechanism: Theorem 3.4 characterizes the bottleneck but doesn't explain why attention-based aggregation outperforms simpler alternatives; no quantitative analysis of what information is recovered from multiple views

Limited forecasting evaluation: only ETTm1 dataset with 30% missingness, single 24-step horizon, and limited baselines (GRU, Cubic only); insufficient to validate claims about generalization to generative tasks

Fundamental bottleneck constraint from Theorem 3.4: global step size bounded by minimum h across heads (NFE ≲ (h_min)^{-1}), limiting potential gains from very heterogeneous multi-scale decompositions; empirically observed diminishing returns at M≈4

Memory overhead under-discussed: Table 3 shows MVC GP requires 1-10× more VRAM than baseline CDEs (375MB vs 155MB on SpokenArabicDigits); while better than Mamba, this non-trivial trade-off deserves emphasis in main text

Incomplete recent method comparisons: Log-Neural CDEs (Walker et al. 2024) included but not deeply analyzed; signature-based methods mentioned but not empirically compared; limited depth in understanding complementarity vs. direct alternatives

Dataset scale limitations: three main UEA benchmarks are relatively small (max 8,800 samples, 315 timesteps); no evaluation on modern large-scale time series benchmarks; supplementary PEMS-SF helps but still limited scope
Reproducibility concern: while hyperparameters provided in appendix, no mention of code availability (may be required for ICML 2026 venue); some implementation details scattered across appendix
